title: Priority-decay bundler for streaming chat: mitigate KV pressure and GPU memory spikes
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Background:
We observe periodic GPU memory spikes and increased KV cache churn during periods of small, high-priority streaming chat turns (interactive assistants). Current continuous-batching groups by arrival window and token budget but does not account for cross-turn KV reuse or bursty priority traffic, causing: 
- KV cache thrashing when many short turns from different sessions are batched together
- Large temporary GPU slab allocations for bundles with heterogeneous sequence lengths
- Increased p99 latency when a high-priority short turn is held behind a batch with slow turns

Goal:
Design and ship a batching heuristic (Priority-Decay Bundler) that reduces KV cache pressure and GPU memory spikes while preserving p50/p95 latency and throughput. The heuristic should be compatible with streaming completions and support graceful fallback to the low-latency path.

Proposed heuristic (summary):
1) Priority decay score: each request is assigned a numeric score = base_priority + freshness_boost - age_decay. Freshness_boost favors recently active sessions (KV hot paths). Age_decay ensures older queued requests slowly drop in bundling priority to prevent starvation.
2) KV affinity tag: compute a lightweight fingerprint of recent KV keys (first N tokens of conversation embedding or session id). During batch formation prefer grouping requests sharing KV affinity to maximize KV reuse and reduce cache misses.
3) Memory-aware slab reservation: estimate per-request GPU slab using sequence length histogram + kv-shared factor. Reserve slim slabs for groups with high kv-affinity, and reserve an emergency slab budget for heterogenous bundles.
4) Time-window adaptivity: use a small adaptive micro-window (2-15ms) for high-priority traffic and a larger window for background traffic. Window size chosen by recent p95 latency and GPU occupancy signals.
5) Short-turn fast-lane: if a request is tagged as latency-critical and short (<= 12 tokens), route to fast-lane which can either preempt the current forming batch or be scheduled immediately if emergency slab budget is available.
6) KV prefetch hinting: when grouping by affinity, optionally prefetch KV entries into on-GPU caches ahead of kernel launch to reduce first-token latency for reused sessions.

Acceptance criteria:
- p99 GPU memory spike frequency reduced by >= 35% on internal bursty-chat trace (compare baseline to new heuristic)
- KV cache miss rate reduced by >= 25% for conversational workloads with high session reuse
- p95 latency change within +/- 5% for representative mixed traffic; p50 latency improved for high-priority short turns
- No regression in throughput (tokens/sec) beyond 5% for standard benchmark suite
- Feature gated and can be turned off at route or account level

Design trade-offs and notes:
- Affinity fingerprinting must be cheap: computing embeddings is expensive. We will use a small session-level fingerprint (SHA-1 of session id + last-turn token-range) or lightweight hashing of the last 32 tokens.
- Prefetching KV increases memory pressure if misgrouped: only enabled when affinity confidence >= threshold.
- Fast-lane reduces batching efficiency; we limit fast-lane to <10% of requests per GPU and fall back to normal bundling for larger requests.
- This heuristic adds complexity to the batcher; start with a staged rollout (internal-only -> canary -> all routable)

Implementation plan:
- Phase 1 (spike): implement prototype scorer and affinity fingerprint in the simulated batcher and run offline replay on production traces (1 week).
- Phase 2 (engine): integrate scorer into live continuous-batcher, add GPU slab estimator and emergency slab budget control (2 weeks).
- Phase 3 (telemetry + policies): add metrics: batch_affinity_ratio, kv_reuse_rate, emergency_slab_invocations, fast_lane_rate, per-route p95/p99 memory spikes. Implement route-level gates and config. (1 week).
- Phase 4 (canary + rollout): internal canary, collect metrics, iterate on thresholds, then staged customer rollouts (1-2 weeks).

Testing and benchmarks:
- Replayer: use production streaming traces with labels (interactive-assistant/high-priority) and compare baseline bundler vs new bundler.
- Unit tests: deterministic scoring, affinity grouping deterministic under same fingerprint, slab estimator math.
- Perf tests: 3 GPU pool sizes, mixed seq lengths, and synthetic KV-hot vs KV-cold traffic.

Rollout and monitoring:
- Feature flag per-route and per-account.
- Dashboards: show before/after KV-miss-rate, GPU-mem-spike-count, p95 latency, tokens/sec.
- Safety: revert to baseline bundler automatically if p99 memory spike rate crosses threshold or error rate increases by >3% in 5-minute window.

Risks:
- Incorrect affinity fingerprinting could reduce batch efficiency and increase misses. Mitigation: conservative thresholds and disable prefetch by default.
- Fast-lane starvation could hurt background throughput; mitigation: strict rate limits and backpressure.

comments: 2026-03-01 - Triage: Initial idea captured during SRE postmortem for p99 memory spike. Assigned to Rafa; estimate 8.
2026-03-03 - Design review: Decided on session-id based affinity fingerprint to avoid embedding compute. Priya asked for clear telemetry for KV reuse.
2026-03-05 - Spike complete: Offline replay shows affinity grouping reduces KV misses by ~28% on test trace. Uploaded replay results: https://drive.redwood.ai/drive/affinity-spike-2026-03-05
2026-03-07 - Engineering: Implemented scorer and slab estimator in the dev batcher. Microbenchmarks added to perf-suite. PR opened: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4567
2026-03-09 - Telemetry: Added batch_affinity_ratio and emergency_slab_invocations to metrics. Initial canary scheduled for 2026-03-12.

2026-03-10 - Blocker discovered: Prefetch path caused transient OOM in one internal cluster when affinity threshold misclassified. Temporarily disabled prefetch in canary. Plan: add tighter threshold and circuit breaker.
